Latin_full_paragraph: Sentius itaque his sermonibus usus est senatu delectabiliter audiente et equitibus romanis qui presentes erant. Quo facto quidam trebellius maximus insiliens, anulum de digito traxit habentem lapidem clusum in quo forma gai caelata uidebatur, quem ille sibimet studio dicendi quae suadebat impleri fuerat oblitus auferre et celeratura quidem est agnita. Nox autem continuo subsecuta. Chereas uero cum signum a consulibus petisset, et illi libertatis ei dedissent miraculum fuit cunctis et uelut incredulitas, qui a reuersa uideretur ad consulens haec potestas. Hi siquiidem antequam tyrannis inuaderet ciuitatem rebus ciuitatibus militaribus praesidebant qui senatui consentiebant. Erant enim cohortes quattuor quibus uincere sine principe magis quam sub tyrannide conplacebat. Milites itaque cum tribunis abibant et populi discedebant laeti. Hanc spem habentes atque cogitationem quasi ipsi gubernationem rei publicę rursus adquirerent, et nequaquam alio subiacerent, inter quos chereas praecipuis existebat.

approved_adjacent_extents.English: And this was the purport of Sentius's oration, which was received with pleasure by the senators, and by as many of the equestrian order as were present. And now one Trebellius Maximus rose up hastily, and took off Sentius's finger a ring, which had a stone, with the image of Caius engraven upon it, and which, in his zeal in speaking, and his earnestness in doing what he was about, as it was supposed, he had forgotten to take off himself. This sculpture was broken immediately. But as it was now far in the night, Cherea demanded of the consuls the watchword, who gave him this word, Liberty. These facts were the subjects of admiration to themselves, and almost incredible; for it was a hundred years since the democracy had been laid aside, when this giving the watchword returned to the consuls; for before the city was subject to tyrants, they were the commanders of the soldiers. But when Cherea had received that watchword, he delivered it to those who were on the senate's side, which were four regiments, who esteemed the government without emperors to be preferable to tyranny. So these went away with their tribunes. The people also now departed very joyful, full of hope and of courage, as having recovered their former democracy, and were no longer under an emperor; and Cherea was in very great esteem with them.
